I am a 45-year-old farmer in Quzhou County, and I have never been to school. I cannot read or write, but I have been working this land since I was a boy, and I know what it can do. My family has about 8 mu of good flat land on the North China Plain, with a well for irrigation.

This year, like every year, I will grow **winter wheat** and **summer maize** on the same 8 mu. That is what everyone around here does — my father did it, my neighbors do it, and the seed seller at the market expects it. Wheat gives us flour for our own steamed buns and noodles, and whatever we do not eat we can sell. Maize is planted right after the wheat comes off in June; it grows fast over the summer and gives us grain to feed our pigs and chickens, plus cash when we sell the surplus. I have thought about cotton, but I see the others spraying chemicals every few days and still worrying about price swings. No — wheat and maize are steady, and I understand them.

For the **winter wheat** that is already in the ground from last October, I used the rotary tiller before sowing to break up the soil, just like always. I bought improved wheat seed from the shop — the kind called Luyuan502 or something similar, the same kind my cousin uses. I put down compound fertilizer at sowing and topdressed with urea when the wheat greened up after winter. I will irrigate four times from my well: once to help it through the last cold days, once at jointing when the stems shoot up, once when the heads are flowering, and once more when the grains are filling. The bugs and weeds come every year, so I will spray pesticide three times — herbicide once, and insecticide twice when the aphids show up. I expect about 1,050 jin per mu, maybe a bit more if the spring rains behave.

After the wheat harvest in early June, I will plant **summer maize** the same day or the next. There is no time to waste — the summer is short. I will not till the soil again; I will plant the maize directly into the wheat stubble with the no-till planter. I use hybrid seed, Denghai605, because everyone says it yields well and stands up to the summer storms. I spread compound fertilizer at planting, and that is usually enough nitrogen for maize. Maize does not need as much water as wheat, so I will irrigate twice — once when it is knee-high, and once when the tassels come out. I will spray pesticide three times to keep the borers and weeds down. If all goes well, I should get about 1,100 jin per mu.

I do what the land and the weather tell me to do. I watch my neighbors, I listen to the old farmers at the village gate, and I buy the same seeds and fertilizer they do. That is how I have always farmed, and that is how I will farm this year.
